titleText.es: Nunca vemos viajeros en el tiempo porque todos descubren que es un gran error. Esto también es la causa por la que hae poco tu amigo del laboratorio de pronto empezó a parecer un año más viejo.
titleText.en: We never see any time travelers because they all discover it's a huge mistake. This is also why your friend at the lab suddenly looked about a year older recently.
titleText.noteEn: Both title attributes are preserved exactly; the Spanish archive really prints the typo hae where standard Spanish would use hace. The visible raster localizes the official impact sound WHAM as PLUM. OCR hallucinated 2517 from drawing strokes on the workbench, omitted the panel-two ¿SÍ? and the last-panel ¿QUÉ HAY?, read PLUM as puM and the last HOLA as QUE, dropped the I from IDEA, and misread GUAU, TÚ, and accented ALGÚN.

excludedUnits.rationale: Rob is a personal name rather than Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Eres already identifies one familiar listener, so tú is stated to emphasize the surprising identity of that listener.
Eres is a form of ser because the statement identifies who the other person is; yo names that identity.

regions.labelEs: ESTÁS A PUNTO DE TENER UNA IDEA SOBRE UNA MÁQUINA DEL TIEMPO.

applications.explanationEn: Estás changes for one familiar listener, a punto de marks the imminent action, and tener stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Máquina, del, and tiempo form the established Spanish expression for a time machine.
The single confirmation word becomes a surprised yes-or-no question through its intonation and question marks.

excludedUnits.rationale: Rob is a personal name rather than Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Qué carries a written accent because it asks a direct question.
Qué and hay form the complete casual greeting rather than a request to list existing things.

regions.labelEs: ESTO SUCEDE EN ALGÚN LUGAR MÁS O MENOS UNA VEZ AL MES.

applications.explanationEn: The three fixed words mark the following frequency as approximate rather than exact.
Una vez supplies ‘once,’ al introduces the repeating masculine time period, and mes names that period.

cards.noteEn: Guau can express surprise or admiration. The same spelling can imitate a dog's bark in a different setting.

cards.promptEs: máquina del tiempo · yo futuro · impedir la idea · una vez al mes
cards.questionEn: What time-travel loop creates the joke?
cards.answerEn: A future Rob travels back to stop his earlier self from inventing a time machine, hits him with a bat, and takes his place. The caption suggests that versions of this self-intervention happen to would-be inventors somewhere roughly once a month.
cards.noteEn: Earlier Rob recognizes the visitor as his future self. Future Rob says the invention idea is imminent and stops it with the bat, creating a causal paradox: the trip depends on the time machine whose invention he prevents. In the final panel the older visitor has taken earlier Rob's place and hidden the bat behind the desk; the official title text's suddenly older lab friend points to that replacement. The caption generalizes the episode rather than saying that the same man repeats it monthly.

cards.questionEn: Why might Spanish say tú or yo when the verb already tells you who acts?
cards.answerEn: Say the subject pronoun to add emphasis, contrast, or clarity; otherwise Spanish often leaves it out.
cards.noteEn: A verb form such as eres already points to “you.” Adding tú can stress that particular person, especially in a contrast or a surprised question. The pronoun may appear after the verb.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.answerEn: me; myself (self-reference rather than a sentence subject)
cards.noteEn: Yo normally means “I” when it is the subject of a verb. When someone identifies, labels, or addresses their own self, natural English may use “me” or “myself,” while Spanish still uses yo.

example.es: La persona de la foto soy yo.
example.en: The person in the photo is me.

cards.promptEs: estar a punto de + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action is just about to happen?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of estar, then a punto de, then the action verb in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form.
cards.noteEn: Only estar changes for the person and time: estoy, estás, está, and so on. A punto de stays together, and the following action verb remains unchanged. The plus sign means ‘followed by.’

example.es: La película está a punto de empezar.
example.en: The film is about to start.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of estar a punto de
cards.noteEn: A belongs to the fixed pattern estar a punto de, which says that an action is just about to happen.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of estar a punto de
cards.noteEn: Punto usually means ‘point,’ but within estar a punto de it helps form the meaning ‘be about to.’

example.es: El tren está a punto de llegar.
example.en: The train is about to arrive.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links estar a punto to the imminent action
cards.noteEn: In estar a punto de, de is required immediately before the action verb in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form.
Idea ends in -a but is a feminine noun: una idea.

cards.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish expression for a machine that travels through time?
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. The expression keeps del tiempo after máquina; Spanish does not normally build this noun pair by placing tiempo directly before máquina.

example.es: La novela incluye una máquina del tiempo.
example.en: The novel includes a time machine.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of máquina del tiempo (‘time machine’)
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. Spanish keeps it between máquina and tiempo in the conventional expression máquina del tiempo.

cards.answerEn: really?; is that so? (asking for confirmation)
cards.noteEn: Sí normally means ‘yes.’ Said as a short question, it can echo surprising information and ask the other person to confirm it.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.
Plum is sound-imitating writing used for a sudden heavy impact or fall.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?
How can you casually ask someone ‘What's up?’
cards.answerEn: Use ¿Qué hay? as a casual greeting or conversation opener.
cards.noteEn: Qué carries an accent because it asks a question, and hay normally means ‘there is’ or ‘there are.’ Together, ¿Qué hay? literally asks what there is, but in casual conversation it works like ‘What's up?’ The tone is informal.

cards.answerEn: is up; is going on (as part of ¿qué hay?)
cards.noteEn: Hay ordinarily means ‘there is’ or ‘there are.’ In the fixed casual question ¿Qué hay?, it helps ask ‘What's up?’ or ‘What's going on?’ rather than literally asking for an inventory.
After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.
Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.
Sucede is a present form of suceder for one event or situation. It says that the event happens or takes place.

cards.answerEn: some; some day/time (before a masculine noun)
cards.noteEn: Alguno shortens to algún directly before a masculine singular noun: algún día, algún libro.

example.en: Some neighbor will have the key.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins más o menos
cards.noteEn: Más, o, and menos combine as más o menos to mean ‘more or less,’ ‘roughly,’ or ‘approximately.’

example.es: Tarda más o menos una hora.

cards.questionEn: How can you say that a number, time, or description is approximate?
cards.answerEn: Use más o menos before or after the approximate information.
cards.noteEn: The literal pieces are ‘more or less,’ but together they often work like ‘roughly,’ ‘about,’ or ‘approximately.’

example.es: El viaje dura más o menos dos horas.
example.en: The trip takes about two hours.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of más o menos
cards.noteEn: Más, o, and menos combine as más o menos to mean ‘more or less,’ ‘roughly,’ or ‘approximately.’

example.es: Llegarán más o menos a las ocho.
example.en: They will arrive at about eight.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes más o menos
cards.noteEn: Más, o, and menos combine as más o menos to mean ‘more or less,’ ‘roughly,’ or ‘approximately.’

example.es: Son más o menos veinte personas.

cards.noteEn: Here una gives the number of occasions rather than introducing an unspecified thing.

cards.promptEs: una vez al + período de tiempo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens once in each stated time period?
cards.answerEn: Use una vez al before a masculine time period, such as día, mes, or año.
cards.noteEn: Una vez supplies ‘once.’ Al is a + el and introduces the repeating period. With a feminine period, use a la instead, as in una vez a la semana.

example.es: La reunión ocurre una vez al año.
example.en: The meeting happens once a year.

cards.noteEn: In a frequency expression, al combines a + el before a masculine time period: una vez al mes means ‘once per month.’

example.es: Voy al médico dos veces al año.
example.en: I go to the doctor twice a year.
